reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: The most common lethal skeletal dysplasia, typically incompatible with survival beyond the neonatal period because of a severely small thorax and pulmonary hypoplasia
Caused by activating variants in FGFR3 that produce far stronger receptor signalling than achondroplasia, arising almost always de novo in an autosomal dominant manner
Features include extreme micromelia, a narrow bell-shaped thorax, a large head with frontal bossing and depressed nasal bridge, and redundant skin folds on the limbs
Type I is characterised by curved, short femora resembling telephone receivers with a normally shaped skull, whereas type II features straight femora with a cloverleaf skull deformity
Radiographs show platyspondyly with markedly flattened vertebrae, short ribs, small squared iliac bones, and short curved or straight long bones
Prenatal ultrasound often detects severe limb shortening, a small chest, and polyhydramnios, prompting molecular confirmation and genetic counselling
Management is directed toward confirming the diagnosis, counselling, and compassionate perinatal care given the lethal prognosis
reference.pathophysiology: Thanatophoric dysplasia is caused by strongly activating variants in FGFR3. The resulting profound constitutive receptor signalling severely disrupts growth-plate chondrocyte proliferation and endochondral ossification, producing extreme limb shortening and a markedly hypoplastic thoracic cage. The small thorax restricts lung development, and the consequent pulmonary hypoplasia is the usual cause of neonatal death. The same signalling excess also affects cortical brain development in some cases, contributing to the cloverleaf skull and neurological abnormalities seen particularly in type II.
additionalInvestigations: Prenatal ultrasound and, where available, fetal MRI to characterise limb, thorax, and skull findings
Postnatal skeletal survey demonstrating platyspondyly, short ribs, and characteristic femoral shape
FGFR3 molecular testing to confirm the diagnosis and subtype
Fetal or neonatal autopsy with placental examination when consent is given
Genetic counselling with discussion of recurrence risk and prenatal options
Neuroimaging where cloverleaf skull or neurological abnormality is present
redFlags: Severe respiratory failure at birth from pulmonary hypoplasia
Prenatal detection of a severely constricted thorax and extreme micromelia indicating a likely lethal dysplasia
Cloverleaf skull with signs of raised intracranial pressure
Feeding and airway compromise requiring urgent palliative planning
reference.prognosis: Thanatophoric dysplasia is almost universally lethal in the perinatal period, with most affected infants dying shortly after birth from respiratory failure. Rare survivors with intensive respiratory support have severe disability and profound growth restriction.
pitfalls: Confusing it with severe achondroplasia or homozygous achondroplasia without molecular confirmation
Underestimating the lethality and delaying appropriate counselling and palliative planning
Missing the distinction between type I and type II femoral and skull morphology
Failing to offer autopsy and genetic counselling to inform recurrence risk
